title: The Tragedies of Ar-Raji & Bi'r Ma'una
subtitle: The Martyrdom of the Reciters and the Steadfastness of Khubayb
summary: Al-Raji' and the killing of Asim and Khubayb in Bukhari 4086; the reciters at Bi'r Ma'unah, seventy in Bukhari 4090, with a classical report of forty; Haram ibn Milhan's words in Bukhari 4091; and the qunut in Sahih Muslim, Book of Mosques, Hadith 677.

sections.text: The Perilous Fourth Year of the Hijrah

In the fourth year following the migration to Madinah, the Muslim community faced an excruciating test of faith and resilience. While the direct threat of Quraysh was temporarily blunted at Hamra' al-Asad, predatory desert tribes perceived the losses at Uhud as a sign of vulnerability. Treachery and deceit began to surround the nascent state, leading to two devastating catastrophes within mere weeks of each other: the ambush at Ar-Raji and the slaughter at the Well of Ma'una.

Delegates from the tribes of 'Adal and Al-Qarah arrived in Madinah claiming that people in their territories were eager to embrace Islam and learn the recitation of the Qur'an. Trusting their plea, the Prophet ﷺ dispatched a small delegation of noble teachers and reciters under the leadership of Asim ibn Thabit. When the party reached the watering hole of Ar-Raji in the territory of Hudhayl, the deceit was revealed. Approximately one hundred archers from the Banu Lihyan ambushed them. The Muslims climbed a rocky hillock and refused to surrender unconditionally. Asim fought valiantly until he fell as a martyr, praying that Allah protect his body from desecration by the idolaters—a prayer answered when a swarm of hornets shielded his remains.

Three companions were taken captive by trickery. One, Abdullah ibn Tariq, resisted when they attempted to bind him and was killed on the road. The remaining two, Khubayb ibn 'Adi and Zayd ibn al-Dathinah, were brought to Makkah and sold to clans seeking revenge for their relatives slain at Badr. Khubayb was purchased by the sons of Al-Harith ibn Amir and imprisoned until the sacred months had elapsed.
The Dignity of Khubayb & The Two Rak'ahs

During his captivity, witnesses among his captors observed miraculous signs of divine favor; Mawiyyah, a household servant, reported seeing Khubayb eating fresh grapes while bound in chains in a city where no fruit was in season. When the day of his public execution arrived at Al-Tan'im outside the sanctuary borders, Khubayb made a singular request: permission to offer two brief units of prayer before God. Granted his wish, he prayed with sublime serenity, then turned to his executioners saying: 'By Allah, were it not that you might imagine I lingered out of fear of death, I would have prayed far longer.' He thus established the enduring Islamic tradition of offering two rak'ahs before unjust execution.

Tied to the execution post, Abu Sufyan mocked him: 'Would you not love that Muhammad were in your place while you were safe with your family?' Khubayb's reply resonated across Arabian history: 'By Allah, I would not desire to be safe with my family and children while a single thorn pricks Muhammad ﷺ where he stands!' Looking up toward the heavens, he uttered his moving supplication of trust in Allah's all-seeing justice.

Shortly thereafter, an even greater calamity struck. Abu Bara' Amir ibn Malik, a prominent elder of the Banu Amir tribe of Najd, visited the Prophet ﷺ. Although he declined to embrace Islam, he requested that a group of companions be sent to teach his people, guaranteeing them his personal covenant of sanctuary and protection (jiwar). Relying on this solemn Arabian pledge, the Prophet dispatched forty—or by some accounts seventy—of his most learned companions, known as the Qurra' (the Reciters of the Qur'an), under the leadership of Al-Mundhir ibn Amr.

When the party reached Bi'r Ma'una, they sent Haram ibn Milhan to deliver the Prophet's letter to Amir ibn al-Tufayl, the nephew of Abu Bara'. Amir did not even read the message; he signaled a man who crept behind Haram and speared him through the back. As the blade pierced through his chest and blood gushed forth, Haram wiped the blood upon his face and cried out with transcendent triumph: 'Allahu Akbar! Fuztu wa Rabbil-Ka'bah!' ('Allah is the Greatest! By the Lord of the Ka'bah, I have succeeded!'). Amir ibn al-Tufayl then summoned neighboring clans of Sulaym—Usayyah, Ri'l, and Dhakwan—who surrounded the camp and slaughtered the teachers almost to the last man.

When news of the twin massacres reached Madinah, profound grief engulfed the Prophet ﷺ. Anas ibn Malik recounted that he had never seen the Messenger of Allah ﷺ grieve over any tragedy as deeply as he grieved over the righteous reciters of Bi'r Ma'una. For thirty consecutive mornings during the dawn prayer (Fajr), the Prophet stood in prolonged supplication (Qunut al-Nawazil), invoking divine justice against the treacherous perpetrators who had broken their sacred covenants and murdered unarmed teachers of light.

وَلَا تَحْسَبَنَّ الَّذِينَ قُتِلُوا فِي سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ أَمْوَاتًا ۚ بَلْ أَحْيَاءٌ عِندَ رَبِّهِمْ يُرْزَقُونَ
'And never think of those who have been killed in the cause of Allah as dead. Rather, they are alive with their Lord, receiving provision.' (Surah Aal-Imran 3:169)

The blood of Ar-Raji and Bi'r Ma'una was not shed in vain; it carved into the consciousness of early Islam that preserving the divine revelation demands absolute loyalty and willingness to sacrifice all, inspiring future generations with an enduring standard of moral courage.

references.title: The Holy Quran
references.author: Surah Aal-Imran (3:169–171)
references.notes: Quranic affirmation that martyrs are alive with their Lord, rejoicing in His grace.

references.title: Sahih al-Bukhari
references.author: Imam Muhammad ibn Isma'il al-Bukhari (d. 256 AH)
references.notes: 4086 is the expedition of Asim and the killing of Khubayb. 4090 reports seventy reciters killed at Bi'r Ma'unah and qunut for a month. 4091 and 4092 report Haram ibn Milhan's words, 'I have succeeded, by the Lord of the Ka'bah.' 4095 is the qunut and the later-lifted verse. Numbers in the old span 4090–4096 that were not opened are not cited.

references.title: Sahih Muslim
references.author: Imam Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj (d. 261 AH)
references.source: Kitab al-Masajid wa Mawadi' al-Salah (Book of Mosques and Places of Prayer), Hadith 677
references.notes: Anas: qunut for thirty mornings after Bi'r Ma'unah, against Ri'l, Dhakwan, Lihyan, and Usayyah, and a verse later abrogated. This is not the Book of Leadership. The count of seventy is in Bukhari 4090. A report of forty belongs to the sirah, so the summary does not treat one number as the only one.
